Both countries have roughly the same population. The IPv4 problem has been swept under the rug with CGNAT and a normal person doesn't even notice it. But it sucks. Forget having a dedicated IP, even on a broadband connection, you don't get a public IP that's truly yours. According to IPInfo[1], there are around 1,000 users sharing my IP. I get flagged for malicious activity, and online gaming is impossible without a Tailscale relay.

Of course, much of this comes down to the bad luck (+ policies) of developing late, when most IPv4 blocks had already been allocated. But it's pretty unfair how US DoD, Apple, Ford, and others [1] are sitting on enormous IPv4 blocks they'll probably never fully use, and may never sell. Meanwhile I am sharing a single public IP with a thousand strangers.

[1]: https://ipinfo.io/223.233.77.184

[2]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_assigned_/8_IPv4_addre...

From a Georgist perspective, IPv4 is actually a form of land (it's a finite "natural resource", although that's not quite proper), and you could make a case for "land rent" being taxed on the addresses. This is the same as radio broadcast frequencies, web addresses, actual land, un-mined gold/oil/coal/whatever, and other finite natural resources that create monopolistic tendencies.
IPv6 got some real traction in the last decade. From around 10% adoption up to 50%. It's not dead, like many are claiming. It works fine, just keep implementing it.
The fact that we have yet to fully deprecate IPv4 should be considered a great failure in the tech industry's competence.

The only thing that surprised me was that Canada was so small compared to other Western countries. But I suppose that might be an artifact. The map shows IPv4 proportional to land area, but a "fair" allocation would have IPv4 proportionate to population, not land area, and I'd assume Canada is (overall) less densely populated than most other developed countries.

Ran across a comment a while ago on some fun "IPv6 math":

    On the surface of the Earth [land+water], there are 8.4 IPv4 addresses per km². Not counting the oceans, that would be 28 IPv4 addresses per km² land.

    IPv6 gives 10¹⁷ addresses per mm² (yes, square millimetre).

    In terms of volume, 10⁸ IPv6 addresses per mm³ throughout the Earth.
* Via: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=28326806#unv_28331245

A second way of thinking about it:

* Stars in the Milky Way: 400 Billion

* Galaxies in the universe: 2 Trillion

* So (4x10¹¹)x(2x10¹²) = 8x10²³ stars in the universe.

* Size of IPv6 address space: 3.4x10³⁸

* Find the ratio between addresses and stars: 3.4x10³⁸ / 8x10²³

IPv6 offers about 430 trillion times more addresses than estimated stars in the universe. From Tom Coffee's presentation "An Enterprise IPv6 Address Planning Case-Study":

Fun fact: At the Assembly demoparty, every system wired to the party network receives a dedicated, publicly routable IPv4 address. It's a lot of fun, but can lead to some interesting moments. One year as I was getting my setup ready, I had a bit of a heart dropping moment when I realized that the raspberry pi I use to bridge ethernet to my Mac Plus over SCSI, the very same one that usually lives on my home network with all kinds of exciting old daemons running, was in fact reachable on the public internet!

The only real use-case for IPv6 is self-hosting, and that's just very niche. Other than that the arguments in favor of IPv6 turn to stuff like latency and network complexity. That's not nothing, but it won't make anyone change ISP, and so ISPs don't have to care about it.

From the ISP's POV a complex IPv4 network plus a simple IPv6 network is more work than just having a complex IPv4 network. IPv6 is optional, and IPv4 isn't.

The only way I can imagine IPv6 succeeding is if somehow big websites decide to slow things down for IPv4 users enough that they complain to their ISPs.

I still think we should just extend the length of IPv4. In my proposed system, existing addresses would become a subnet of the new set.

Eg 192.168.0.1 becomes 0.0.0.0.192.168.0.1

And then we dish out all the new address space. You would get the network providers to handle address conversion until software and hardware has been updated. Because all the existing addresses are reserved in the new set, it doesn’t affect them.

Keeps all the nice parts of IPv4, doesn’t require everyone to switch to an entirely new system, backwards compatible with existing hardware/software. Problem solved.
